card.hook: Picture rows of tiled roofs rolling away from you, with old stone paving leading your eye straight in. That's Gyeongbokgung, and it's so big and open that your photos get depth almost by accident.
card.stand_here: Head to the phone icon at Gyeongbokgung Palace, about 70 m south of the subject. Face north towards the palace.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the main view. Go to 0.5x when you want a whole courtyard and the buildings around it in one shot. Then try 2x or 5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) for painted beams, roof ends and carved details.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the building, then slide the brightness down a touch if the sky is bright, so the roof colours don't wash out.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually means softer light and fewer people. The palace is open at night for part of the year, so check the official site for dates before you plan an evening visit.
card.selfie_here: Pose in the courtyard in front of Geunjeongjeon, the main throne hall, with the hall behind you so it fills the frame. Use the front camera, or 0.5x if you want more of the building in. For a quieter backdrop, try the big open field in front of Jibokjae Hall and Parujeong Pavilion, with the buildings behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to shoot from the open square in front of Gwanghwamun Gate, so they can fit you, the whole gate and the mountain behind it in one frame (one guide suggests blue hour, when the gate is lit).
card.rules_and_safety: Check the official site for current visiting and entry details before you go.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot of a courtyard, then find three close details, like a painted eave, a doorway and a bit of stonework, and see if you can spot the pattern they share.
card.good_to_know: Gyeongbokgung was the first royal palace of the Joseon dynasty, established in 1395. Hangul, the Korean script, was developed here during Sejong the Great's reign. The palace was burned down in 1592, rebuilt in the 1860s, and by 1945 only 40 pre-colonial buildings remained, though restoration since the 1980s has recreated dozens more.

card.hook: Picture a 600-year-old tiled roof sitting calmly in the middle of buses, office towers and market streets. That clash is the whole picture, and you get the best look at it from above.

card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to catch the station, the streets and the gate together. If the gate looks small, try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) rather than walking away from the railing. Use zoom 0.5x only if you want the walkway and the city in the same shot.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the gate on one of the lines, and let the streets lead towards it.
card.best_time: Go in the evening or at night, when the gate is lit up and the city lights add depth. Switch on night mode and rest your elbows on the railing to keep the phone steady.
card.selfie_here: Head to the front of Sungnyemun Gate, next to the costumed guards at the entrance. Use the front camera, hold it a little low and keep the gate over your shoulder. Visitors say the guards make a great backdrop, and one review says they're there during the day.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to a passer-by and ask them to stand on Sungnyemun Plaza in front of the stone base, so the arch and both roofs fit in one frame with you in front.
card.rules_and_safety: The gate sits in the middle of a busy road, so cross using the traffic signals. It's closed on Mondays, and the closing time varies between sources, so check before you go. The gate's grounds may close to visitors at certain times, so check the official site too.
card.challenge: Find the shot where the gate's roof sits on a gridline and a bus or taxi drives through the bottom of the frame: old Seoul meets new Seoul.
card.good_to_know: Sungnyemun, also called Namdaemun or the South Great Gate, was first built in 1398 and rebuilt in 1447. It became South Korea's National Treasure No. 1 in 1962. A fire destroyed the wooden upper storey in February 2008, and the gate reopened in May 2013 after a long restoration.

card.hook: Picture a lane so narrow your elbows have opinions, with steam rising off bowls of handmade noodle soup and colourful toppings piled right at the front. That's Kalguksu Alley, and it's the best snapshot of Namdaemun Market.
card.stand_here: Stand in Kalguksu Alley, the narrow lane of noodle stalls inside Namdaemun Market. Face down the lane so the steaming bowls and colourful ingredients sit in the foreground.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the lane scene. Drop to zoom 0.5x when the aisle gets tight and crowded, and try zoom 2x or higher (depending on your phone) for stall details, so you're not leaning into anyone's space.
card.make_it_pop: Tap a mid-tone area, then drag the slider down a touch to make it slightly darker so bright signs don't wash out.
card.best_time: Go earlier in the day, when it usually means fewer people and easier framing. The market has long been known for its morning trade. Daylight keeps the colours true, so save night mode for after dark.
card.selfie_here: Try the spot under the market's Gate 5 sign, where the name board hangs over a street lined with noodle stalls and optical shops. Use the front camera at 0.5x and hold the phone a little low so the sign sits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: If you'd like a full-body shot with the old gate, ask someone to shoot from in front of Sungnyemun Gate on the plaza, where the stone base, the arch and both roofs fit in at once, while you stand in front of the gate.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos for personal use are fine inside the market, but step to the side so you don't block the walkway, and ask before photographing vendors up close. At Sungnyemun Gate, don't climb or lean on the walls or stone base. The plaza sits in the middle of a wide road, so cross with the signals.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot of the busy lane, then find three close-ups: a pile of goods, a handwritten sign and a vendor's hands.
card.good_to_know: Namdaemun Market opened in 1414, in the Joseon period, which makes it one of the oldest markets in Korea still operating. Fires have destroyed it several times, including one during the Korean War, and each time it was rebuilt to roughly the same size. A 2016 count listed about 5,200 stores and 9,090 workers across roughly 64,600 square metres. It's a working market, so check the official site for opening days and times before you go.

card.hook: A 6.2-metre bronze king sits in the middle of a wide-open square, and the palace gate lines up right behind him. Cities rarely arrange a photo this neatly.
card.stand_here: Walk to the King Sejong statue, roughly 250 metres north of the Admiral Yi Sun-sin statue and its fountain. Stand right in front of the king and face north, so Gwanghwamun Gate and the trees at the far end sit behind him.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the king with the gate behind him. Try zoom 0.5x to fit in more of the square, or zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to bring the gate closer behind the statue.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the statue on one of the vertical lines and keep your phone level so the gate doesn't lean.
card.best_time: One guide says the statue looks even better lit up after dark, so try it at dusk. If you stay for night shots, use night mode and hold the phone steady against your body. Another guide says the morning light is best, and by day the gate and trees show up clearly behind the statue.
card.selfie_here: Try Yukjo Yard (육조마당) on the paved ground of the square, where the pine trees, Gwanghwamun Gate and Bugaksan Mountain are all in view. Use the front camera at zoom 0.5x and keep the scenery over your shoulder. Check your screen to make sure the gate is actually behind you, because you may need to shuffle round a bit.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the southern end of the square facing north, while you stand by the King Sejong statue so the gate and Bugaksan Mountain sit behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: It's an open public square, but events can close or crowd parts of it, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take one shot with the king on a gridline and the gate perfectly level above him. Then try a second with you grinning in front of him, and pick the winner.
card.good_to_know: For centuries this ground was the Street of Six Ministries, home to the royal administrative buildings. The King Sejong statue weighs 20 tons and was unveiled on 9 October 2009. The square was closed for redesign from the end of 2020 and the larger plaza reopened on 6 August 2022, so older photos online may not match what you see.

card.hook: Most people shoot N Seoul Tower from the top of the hill. Walk up Huam-ro instead and the tower seems to climb the road ahead of you, which is a much better Seoul shot.
card.stand_here: Stand on Huam-ro (후암로), on the uphill stretch that leads from Seoul Station exit 11. Face up the road so the tower rises along the slope ahead of you.
card.zoom: Start at 1x and keep the tower in the upper part of the picture. If it looks too small, try 2x.

card.selfie_here: Try the crossing in front of the Samsung Dream Scholarship Foundation on Huam-ro, where you can get yourself and the tower in one frame. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if you want more of the road behind you, and hold the phone low so the tower sits over your shoulder. The wooden viewing decks at the foot of the tower, beside the Locks of Love, are another place to try.
card.ask_someone: Cross the junction in front of the Samsung Dream Scholarship Foundation, stand a little way along the pavement, and ask a passer-by to shoot with the tower rising up the road behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Selfie sticks aren't allowed on the observation deck, and it's best not to use one near edges or high places. Follow any photography rules posted on-site, and check the official site before you go up the tower, as access and rules can change.
card.challenge: Take one shot where the tower looks like it's sitting at the very top of the road, then one where it looks like it's growing out of your head. Keep whichever makes you laugh.
card.good_to_know: N Seoul Tower stands on the summit of Namsan and is 236 metres tall. It began as a broadcasting tower: building started in 1969 and the observation decks were finished in 1975. The public weren't let up until October 1980, and the observation levels reopened as N Seoul Tower in December 2005.

card.zoom: Start at 1x for the lane. Try 2x (if your phone has it) to squeeze the rooftops and the city behind them together, or 0.5x if you want the whole slope in the frame. Try not to go past 2x, because the tile detail goes soft.

card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the lower end of Bukchon-ro 11-gil and shoot up the slope while you pose up the lane, with the hanok rooftops and wooden doors around you.
card.rules_and_safety: People live here, so keep your voice down, stay out of gateways, skip the flash, and don't photograph residents. Obey any 'no photo' signs. If you have a stroller or limited mobility, stick to flatter routes and avoid the stone steps.
card.challenge: Can you get a shot where the roof curves lead your eye straight to N Seoul Tower, with not one person in the frame?
card.good_to_know: Much of what you see was built around the 1920s, when developer Chŏng Segwŏn put up smaller hanok with modern touches like glass windows and electricity. Preservation rules from the late 20th century helped save the area while Seoul redeveloped around it. About 6,100 residents live here and share the streets with millions of visitors a year.

card.hook: Most people come to Gwangjang Market for the sizzling pancakes and never look up. Head up to the Starbucks rooftop and you get a calm, sky-filled view of the market's big Korean-script sign.
card.stand_here: Stand on the third-floor rooftop terrace of Starbucks Gwangjang Market, reached by the spiral corridor. Face the Korean-script signage rising above the red-brick wall, with the sky behind it.
card.zoom: Stay at zoom 1x for the signage and brick wall from the rooftop. Down at the arched 광장시장 entrance sign, switch to zoom 0.5x to catch the busy corridor behind it. In the food alley, try zoom 2x or higher for close-ups of the griddles, so you don't crowd the vendors.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the signage on one of the lines, leave lots of sky above it, and keep the red-brick wall along the bottom of the frame.
card.best_time: Early morning is best for the food alley, because midday is packed. For the rooftop signage shot, late afternoon is worth trying, since the sky behind the sign is the star.
card.selfie_here: Use the Starbucks Gwangjang Market rooftop on the third floor. Face away from the sign so it rises above the roofline behind you, then use the front camera (zoom 0.5x if your phone has it) to fit more of it in.
card.ask_someone: Near the main entrance on the Changgyeonggung-ro side (from Jongno 5-ga Station Exit 8), stand where the market name sign is visible and ask a passer-by to step back and shoot you with it behind you; check the angle on arrival.
card.rules_and_safety: Ask vendors' permission before photographing them. The rooftop is inside a café, so check the official site to see whether you can go up without buying anything.
card.challenge: In the food alley, take one photo of a vendor's hands at work on the griddle, with no faces, and try it as a Live Photo to catch the sizzle.
card.good_to_know: Gwangjang Market began in 1905 as Dongdaemun Market, set up by Korean merchants as the first market to open every day of the week. It took the name Gwangjang in 1960. Around 65,000 people pass through on a typical day, many hunting for bindaetteok (mung bean pancakes) and mayak gimbap.

card.hook: You'll probably do what everyone does here: step back, step back again, and still not fit all 555 metres in. Don't worry, the lake is there to help.
card.stand_here: Stand at Seokchon Lake (석촌호수) on the east side, right at the lake edge, and face the tower across the water. The tower rises behind the lake and, on a calm day, you get its reflection too.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the tower, the water and the shoreline in together. Switch to 1x for a calmer, more natural view, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the glass top of the tower.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, keep the tower's straight lines upright, and put the water's edge on the lower line so the reflection has room.
card.best_time: Go in late afternoon or at sunset, when the reflection looks its best. After dark the lit-up tower across the water is worth a try too, so use night mode and tuck your elbows in to keep the phone steady.
card.selfie_here: Head to the south-west corner of Seokchon Lake on the lakeside walking path and turn your back to the tower. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x, and hold the phone a little low so the tower stands tall over your shoulder. It's a lovely spot at night when the tower is lit up. Check the exact corner on the map.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the Seokchon Lake promenade facing the tower across the water, and to step back until the whole building fits in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: If you go up Seoul Sky, selfie sticks may be restricted, so check the rules on the day. The glass floor on the 118th floor can feel dizzying, so don't stare down for too long if heights aren't your thing.
card.challenge: Wait for the ripples to settle, then catch the tower and its reflection in one frame, with you tiny at the water's edge.
card.good_to_know: Lotte World Tower is the tallest building in South Korea: 123 storeys, 555 metres, and sixth-tallest in the world. It opened to the public on 3 April 2017, and its pale glass skin is inspired by Korean ceramics. The lake edge is a public park, but the observation decks inside are a separate ticketed visit, so check the official site if you want to go up.

card.hook: Picture a sunken ribbon of calm water and greenery, with downtown Seoul rising on both sides, right where an expressway used to roar. That's Cheonggyecheon, and it's a surprisingly peaceful spot for a city-centre photo.
card.stand_here: Stand in Cheonggye Plaza, the western starting point of the stream, by the red-and-blue Spring sculpture. Face the sculpture so the two-tier waterfall running down into the stream sits behind it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the stream and its banks as you see them. Go to 0.5x when you want the whole channel, the bridges and the buildings above in one frame. Try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out a bridge or a stretch of water further along.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and run the water along a diagonal or the lower third line, so the stream leads the eye into your picture.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning, when the paths are quieter and you can get clear frames of the water. Come back in the evening for a different mood, and use night mode if the light is low, resting your phone against a railing to keep it steady.
card.selfie_here: Take your selfie on Cheonggye Plaza at the waterfall beside the red-and-blue sculpture, with both behind you. Use the front camera, widen it if your phone lets you, and hold it a little low so the landmark shows over your shoulder. For a warmer, more natural look, try the stepping stones with the flowing stream behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to take your photo while you stand on the walkway next to Gwangtonggyo, the second restored bridge, so the arched bridge and the stream fill the frame behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Take care near the water's edge and on the stepping stones, as wet areas can be slippery. Keep a hand on your phone when you lean over a railing, and keep to the paths so you don't block other walkers. Check the official site before you go in case of closures, events or high water.
card.challenge: Catch one frame with stepping stones in the foreground and a bridge arching across the top, and bonus points if nobody walks through it!
card.good_to_know: Cheonggyecheon is a 10.9-kilometre stream running through the middle of downtown Seoul. In the late 1950s it was covered with concrete, and an elevated expressway was built on top, opened in stages between 1969 and 1976. The city began removing the road in 2003, and the stream reopened to the public in September 2005.

card.hook: Picture a street where a hand-painted sign sits right above a steaming food stall, with old tiled rooftops behind it. Insa-dong is like that, and there's even a Starbucks sign written in Korean.
card.stand_here: Stand about 85 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map near 삼일대로, and face west. Take a few frames here, then stroll towards it and keep shooting along Insadong-gil.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for street scenes, so shopfronts and signs look natural. Drop to zoom 0.5x in the narrow alleys, and try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for lanterns, signs and rooftop details.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to keep sign posts and building edges straight, then tap a sign or shopfront and slide it a little darker if bright signs or the sky wash out.
card.best_time: Early on a weekday morning is likely to be calmer. In the evening, lit signs and shop windows can look great, so switch on night mode if your phone has it.
card.selfie_here: Head to the calligraphy sculpture where Insadong-gil meets Yulgok-ro, at the north-west end of the street, and use the front camera with the sculpture and street signs over your shoulder. For an old-Seoul backdrop, try the marble pagoda in Tapgol Park at the far end of Insadong-gil, at zoom 0.5x so more of it fits in behind you.

card.rules_and_safety: Public streets are fine for photos, but ask before photographing people up close or inside shops.
card.challenge: Try a three-layer shot: a shop sign close up, the crowd in the middle and the rooftops peeking out behind.
card.good_to_know: Insa-dong began roughly 500 years ago as a residential area for government officials. It later became Korea's largest market for antiques and artwork, and it still has plenty of antique shops, galleries and traditional stationery shops. It covers about 12.7 hectares, so you can wander it on foot, and Ssamziegil, a handcrafts shopping centre that opened in 2004, is a well-known stop.

card.hook: Most palaces give you one big building to photograph. Changdeokgung gives you a whole spread of tiled roofs, carved gates and stone courtyards, so you'll never run out of pictures.
card.stand_here: Start at the phone icon on the map, about 80 m west of Changdeokgung Palace, and face east. Treat it as your starting spot, then wander the grounds.
card.zoom: Use zoom 1x for most views, and zoom 0.5x in courtyards and by gateways where you can't step back far enough. Try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for roof ends and painted eaves.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the building, then drag the slider to make the picture a little darker if the sky is bright, so the roof tiles and painted wood don't wash out.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon gives softer light on the roofs and fewer harsh shadows in the courtyards. Go as early as the palace allows if you want fewer people in your shots.
card.selfie_here: Head to the wide stone bridge in front of Donhwamun Gate and turn so the two-story wooden gate is over your shoulder, with the trees and flowers along the wall framing you. Use the front camera, or try zoom 0.5x to fit more gate in. For a second selfie, use the platform in front of Injeongjeon throne hall and let the hall rise behind you.
card.ask_someone: Stand at the top of the large staircase between the Tongmyongheon/Yanghwadang and Yeongchunheon/Jipbokheon buildings, facing the trail, and ask your helper to stand below on the steps and shoot upward so the trees fill the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: The staircase has a slippery stone formation just before its first step, so watch your footing. Some parts of the Secret Garden need a booked tour, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Find a doorway that frames a hall beyond it, and get the whole thing level against your gridlines.
card.good_to_know: Changdeokgung was founded in 1405 as Seoul's second palace, after Gyeongbokgung. Its name means "Palace of Prospering Virtue", and many Joseon kings preferred living here to the official main palace. After all the city's palaces burned in 1592 it was rebuilt and served as the main palace for several centuries, and it became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1997.

card.hook: You walk up to DDP, lift your phone, and realise 280 metres of silver curves is never going to fit in one frame. Good news: that's the fun part, so pick a slice and let the curves do the work.
card.stand_here: Stand on Miraero Bridge and turn to face west, so the curved silver facade is framed by the walkway. Want more of the building in the shot? Walk a few steps back.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x for the big sweep, then try 1x for sections of the curves. Zoom 2x-5x (depending on your phone) is great for panel patterns and edges.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the brightest part of the building, then nudge the picture a touch darker so the silver surfaces keep their detail.
card.best_time: Early morning is calmer, with fewer people in your frame. Around dusk and after dark the curves can look striking with the lights on.
card.selfie_here: Head to Oullim Square at the front, face the silver exterior with the front camera, and let the facade fill the background over your shoulder. Around dusk, the LED Rose Garden in front of the building is a glowing foreground if the roses are lit when you arrive.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the far end of the curved Miraero Bridge and shoot back toward the building's entrance while you stand on the bridge in front, using zoom 0.5x to squeeze the building's length into the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos are fine in most public areas, but some exhibitions restrict them, so check the sign at the entrance. Skip the flash, ask before taking close-ups of strangers, and note that one photography guide says drones aren't allowed. Sloped walkways can get slippery in the rain.
card.challenge: Line up one curved edge with a gridline, keep your phone level, and catch a stranger walking through the frame to show how big the building is.
card.good_to_know: DDP was designed by Zaha Hadid and opened on 21 March 2014. The main building is 280 metres long, with three underground levels and four above ground, and its roof is a walkable park. Dongdaemun Stadium stood on this spot from 1925 until 2007, and parts of the old Seoul fortress wall have been restored nearby.

card.hook: Bright painted eaves, hanging lanterns and a golden Buddha you can spot from outside, all in the middle of downtown Seoul. Give yourself a few minutes in the courtyard, because this one rewards slow looking.
card.stand_here: Come in through the Iljumun (the one-pillar gate) and stand in the entrance courtyard, facing the front of the Main Buddha Hall (the Daeungjeon). The hall isn't signposted, so wander the courtyard a little to find your angle.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the hall, the lanterns and the courtyard into one frame. Switch to 1x for a calmer view of the hall front, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the painted eaves and woodwork.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and keep the roofline level so the hall doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Lotus lanterns go up in the weeks before Buddha's Birthday, usually in May, and in the evening they make the courtyard glow, so use night mode then and hold still while it captures. Outside that season there are far fewer lanterns, so come in daylight for the rich colours of the woodwork.
card.selfie_here: Stand in front of the Iljumun Gate at the temple entrance with the gate behind you, and the white paper lanterns hanging from its beams will fill the top of your photo. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone offers it, and keep the gate over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: This is a working temple, so keep to the outdoor areas and stay outside during services. Don't photograph monks, skip the flash, and check the official site for current photography rules.
card.challenge: Find a hanging lantern or a branch of one of the old trees and use it to frame the top of your photo, with the painted hall glowing underneath.
card.good_to_know: A temple was first founded here in 1395, and it became the chief temple of the Jogye Order in 1936. The Main Buddha Hall was built in 1938 from pine wood from Baekdu Mountain. Two trees about 500 years old, a white pine and a Chinese scholar tree, stand in the courtyard.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Come in through the Iljumun (the one-pillar gate) and stand in the entrance courtyard, facing the front of the Main Buddha Hall (the Daeungjeon). The hall isn't signposted, so wander the courtyard a little to find your angle.

card.hook: Gwanghwamun is the easiest classic Seoul photo you'll take, because the wide plaza runs straight at the gate and does the framing for you. You don't even have to go inside the palace.
card.stand_here: Stand in Gwanghwamun Square at the north end, in front of the King Sejong statue, and face the gate. You'll see the whole front of the gate with the open plaza in front, Bugaksan Mountain rising behind it and the bronze statue beside the frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the gate and the plaza together. Then try zoom 2x to fill the frame with the gate, because at 1x it looks small. Only use zoom 0.5x if you walk much closer.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines, put the middle gate opening on the centre line, and keep your phone level so the roofline stays straight.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon gives you the nicest light, and midday light is too strong. Midday is also when the crowds peak, so you'll have to be patient.
card.selfie_here: Try the paved square by the King Sejong statue, where the gate and the mountains frame the view. Use the front camera at zoom 0.5x and check your screen to get the gate over your shoulder, since we couldn't confirm which way to face for a selfie.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to take your photo from the wide stone-paved walkway directly in front of the gate tower, which gives a full-gate frame.
card.rules_and_safety: You can take photos beside the ceremonial guards outside the gate, but don't touch them or their equipment. Follow any on-site instructions about photo sessions, and check the official site before you go for palace entry rules and guard ceremony times.
card.challenge: Find the stone haetae statue in front of the gate and get it big in the foreground, with the gate sitting right behind it.
card.good_to_know: The gate was first completed in 1395 and named by Sejong the Great in 1426. It was destroyed in 1592 and burned again during the Korean War. The wooden version you see now was rebuilt on its original alignment and opened to the public on 15 August 2010, and the nameplate was reworked in 2023 as gold characters on a black field.

card.hook: Picture a long granite wall, street trees arching overhead like a leafy tunnel, and glass towers peeking in at the far end of the path. That's old and new Seoul in one frame, and it's why this wall is so popular.
card.stand_here: Stand on the pavement of Deoksugung Stone Wall Road (덕수궁 돌담길), on the opposite side of the walkway from the wall. Face along the wall so it runs away from you down the path.
card.zoom: Start at 1x so the wall, trees and path look natural. If the pavement feels tight, try 0.5x, but keep the wall away from the edges. Zoom 2x squeezes the wall and trees closer together.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the wall, then drag the slider to make it a little darker if bright sky or patches of sun wash out the leaves.
card.best_time: Late afternoon into dusk gives soft, low light along the wall, and overcast days keep the tones even. Early morning or a rainy day is usually quieter.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera on the pedestrian path beside the palace wall, with the stone wall behind you. Or head inside to the lawn in front of Seokjojeon Hall and put the stone Western-style hall over your shoulder, since it's a favourite spot for hanbok photos.
card.ask_someone: Inside the grounds, ask someone to step well back from the fountain in front of Seokjojeon Hall so the fountain and the building line up in one straight line.
card.rules_and_safety: Stay on the pavement outside, because the road is narrow and has traffic. Inside, some areas can be slippery, so wear comfy shoes. The grounds are ticketed, so check the official site. One guide says photos may be restricted inside buildings like Seokjojeon, so check the signs.
card.challenge: Turn on gridlines and line the top of the wall up with one of them, then see if you can fit a modern tower in the gap at the end of the path.
card.good_to_know: Deoksugung was the main palace of the Korean Empire (1897–1910), and it mixes traditional Korean halls with Western-style buildings. It began as a temporary royal home during the 1592–1598 Imjin War and was renamed Deoksugung in 1907. One scholar estimates it's now only about a third of its peak size, which is why it feels tucked into the modern city.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the pavement of Deoksugung Stone Wall Road (덕수궁 돌담길), on the opposite side of the walkway from the wall. Face along the wall so it runs away from you down the path.

card.hook: Most buildings end somewhere. Jeongjeon, the main hall at Jongmyo Shrine in Seoul, just keeps going: a long row of dark columns under one unbroken roofline, and it's the longest building of traditional design in Korea.
card.stand_here: Stand on the 월대 (Woldae), the edge of the stone terrace in front of Jeongjeon, and face the hall. You get the row of dark columns and the roofline, with the open stone platform in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole length of Jeongjeon in one frame. Switch to 1x for a tidier, less stretched shot of part of the hall, then try 2x or 5x for the columns and roof tiles (higher zooms depend on your phone).
card.make_it_pop: The columns are dark, so tap the building, and if the sky turns white, drag the slider to make it a little darker.
card.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light is usually kinder to the dark columns and the roofline. Visits to the main halls are usually by guided tour, so your time on the terrace may be set by the tour. One guide says the shrine closes on Tuesdays, so check the official site before you go.
card.selfie_here: Stand in the open courtyard in front of Jeongjeon and turn your back to the hall. Use the front camera at 0.5x so the long red-pillared building fills the frame behind your shoulder. If you have a few spare minutes, the stone wall path Seosunra-gil also makes a nice backdrop, with its old wall and trees behind you.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to a friendly passer-by, stand in the courtyard in front of Jeongjeon, and ask them to step back until the whole hall and you both fit in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is not allowed inside Jeongjeon or Yeongnyeongjeon, though courtyards and building exteriors are fine. Selfie sticks are not allowed, so keep it handheld. Keep off any stones marked as the spirit path, and follow the signs elsewhere in the grounds.
card.challenge: Turn on the gridlines and line the roof up with a horizontal one so the hall sits dead level, then see if you can fit a whole building that long into one shot.
card.good_to_know: Jongmyo is the royal ancestral shrine of the Joseon dynasty, where memorial services were held for deceased kings and queens. It joined the UNESCO World Heritage list in 1995. The buildings were rebuilt in 1601 after the older shrine burned down in the Japanese invasions of the 1590s.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the 월대 (Woldae), the edge of the stone terrace in front of Jeongjeon, and face the hall. You get the row of dark columns and the roofline, with the open stone platform in front of you.

card.hook: A quiet old church sitting in the middle of one of Seoul's busiest shopping districts. That clash is the whole reason this spot works, so let the shopfronts into your picture.
card.stand_here: Stand on Myeongdong Shopping Street, where the cathedral lies to the east, about 220 m away. Face east and let the shopfronts on one or both sides frame the spire.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the street and the cathedral together. Try zoom 2x to pull the cathedral closer between the buildings, and use zoom 0.5x only if you want loads of street in the shot.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the cathedral, then slide the brightness down to darker so the lit church doesn't wash out against the night sky.
card.best_time: Go after dark, when the cathedral is lit and the street lights and signs add colour around it. Christmas is extra popular, so expect crowds and give yourself a little patience for a clear gap.
card.selfie_here: Head to the stone steps in the small garden beside the church and climb up toward the spire. Use the front camera at zoom 0.5x with the spire over your shoulder, and the street noise fades behind you. Visiting in December? The big Christmas tree to the right of the entrance is a popular photo stop.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to someone at the foot of the entrance stairs, or on the path to the right of those steps, and stand in front of the cathedral so the whole facade and spire fit in.
card.rules_and_safety: The outside of the cathedral is open to the public all day, but photos inside aren't allowed during services, so check the official site before you go in.
card.challenge: Catch the old and the new in one frame: the spire and a glowing shop sign, with zero people walking through (good luck!).
card.good_to_know: Myeongdong Cathedral is the national cathedral of the Archdiocese of Seoul and the seat of its archbishop. It was dedicated on 29 May 1898, and it was the largest building in Seoul when it was built. The government listed it as Historic Site No. 258 in November 1977.

card.hook: The best-known view of Seoullo 7017 isn't on Seoullo 7017 at all. You're down in the square with the old Seoul Station right in front of you, and the walkway is just a green line across the city scene.
card.stand_here: Stand in 서울역 광장, the square in front of the old Seoul Station building, with the walkway about 140 metres to the east. Face the old station so the building is in front of you and the station bustle sits behind it.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the old station and the walkway in one shot. If the building won't fit, tap 0.5x, and use 2x or more for close-ups of the walkway and its plants.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and put the old station on one third of the frame, then tap the building and drag the slider darker if the sky turns white.
card.best_time: Daytime suits the old station building. Around dusk and into the evening, the lit walkway and the lights of the station and downtown make a more colourful picture, so switch on night mode.
card.selfie_here: Two guides rank the Seoul Station Square viewpoint on the walkway as the top souvenir-photo stop. Stand on the walkway overlooking the square, use the front camera (0.5x if your phone has it), and let the old station building and the busy backdrop sit over your shoulder. The rose-planted Rose Square observation point is a popular second stop, with roses for a romantic setting.
card.rules_and_safety: Opening times and closures can change, so check the official site before you go. We don't know of a selfie-stick rule for the walkway, but some places ban them, so check the signs on site.
card.challenge: Snap the old station with the walkway as a green stripe across the frame, then try to find the same view with a stranger photobombing it in the best possible way.
card.good_to_know: Seoullo 7017 is a raised walkway about 1 kilometre long, built on an old highway overpass that closed in 2015. It sits some 17 metres above the street and is planted with around 24,000 plants. The Dutch firm MVRDV designed it, and it opened in May 2017. The name comes from 1970, when the overpass was dedicated, and 2017, when the walkway opened, and the 17 also counts the walkways connected to it.

card.hook: Picture a red-and-green pavilion with glass office towers looming right behind it, and traffic rolling past at your feet. That's Bosingak, and it gives you old and new Seoul in a single frame.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the subject, in front of the pavilion at the Jongno crossroads. Face the pavilion so the office towers rise behind it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x and keep the whole building in view with the towers behind it. If crowds push you in close, drop to 0.5x. Then step back and try 2x or more to pick out the roof against the trees.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to keep the roofline level, and put the building in the lower half so the towers show above it.
card.best_time: Evening can look atmospheric if the pavilion is lit, and daytime is great for the red and green colours. New Year's Eve around midnight is the famous moment, but it's very crowded.
card.selfie_here: Climb the stone steps and balustrade in front of the pavilion, so the red pillars and green eaves are behind you. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone offers it, and hold the phone a little higher so the roof fits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the pavement across from the pavilion, near Jonggak Station Exit 4, while you stand on the steps so they can fit you and the whole building in.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos are generally fine during the daily bell-ringing and on New Year's Eve, but don't block other people's views. On New Year's Eve, Line 1 trains don't stop at Jonggak Station because of the crowds, so plan another way to arrive.
card.challenge: Take a shot with the pavilion's roofline perfectly level and one tower poking up right behind it, like a hat.
card.good_to_know: Bosingak was first built in 1395 and has been destroyed several times by war and fire. Its bell gave Jongno its name, which means 'bell street'. The bell hanging there now is a replica, and the original from 1468 is in the National Museum of Korea.
